s: Part three.
Error propagation.
By the end of this part, you'll know how a failure should travel from one agent to another, what words it should use, when to retry it, and who is to blame when a gap disappears.
Let's start with a picture.
You send three people to check eight rooms of a building for damp.
One of them cannot get the key to two rooms.
The report that comes back says "no damp in the building."
Every sentence in it is true.
And the report is a lie.
What's the fix?
It's not to make the report sound less sure.
The fix is for that person to come back and say this.
Rooms six and seven not entered.
Key missing.
Someone with the key can do it in ten minutes.
And no reading is not the same as a dry reading.
That is the whole of this part.
Where one agent hands work to another, information is thinnest exactly where it matters most.
And silence reads as good news to everyone downstream.
The technical version.
The notes put it this way.
Hold on to this line.
An error that crosses an agent boundary as prose becomes a rumour.
Picture a coordinator receiving "I was unable to complete the analysis."
What can it decide?
Nothing.
It cannot tell total from partial failure.
It cannot tell whether a retry could help.
And it cannot tell which units went uncovered.
So it does one of the two worst things available.
It retries blindly.
Or it treats the missing result as an absence of findings, and reports success.
There are two layers.
And the exam separates them.
First, the tool layer.
Here the API defines a specific channel.
A tool result block can carry a flag called is_error, set to true, with content describing the failure.
The documentation names three categories.
Tool execution errors.
Invalid tool names.
And server tool errors.
And it says descriptive error content helps the model recover.
On the Model Context Protocol wire, the same flag is spelled isError.
Both spellings are correct, on their own surface.
Second, the agent layer.
Here there is no protocol at all.
There is only the contract you impose on what a subagent returns.
That contract is a structured result.
Let's build it piece by piece.
It has a status, such as partial.
It has a completed section, with the findings that succeeded.
It has a failures list.
Each failure names quite a lot.
The unit of work.
The phase.
An error_class.
An error_code.
A human-readable detail.
A retryable flag.
A retry_would_help_if field, stating the condition under which a retry would help.
The number of attempts.
And a pointer to evidence, such as a log path.
It carries coverage counts.
Units requested.
Units completed.
Units failed.
And it carries a claim_scope.
That's a sentence stating which units were not examined, and that the absence of findings for them is not evidence they are clean.
One more.
If it carries a confidence level, that comes with an explicit basis.
Such as what the data is current as of, and what went unscanned.
Why?
Because a bare confidence level cannot be evaluated.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A research coordinator fans out five search subagents.
Two hit upstream timeouts.
They catch the exception, and return an empty findings list with status success.
The synthesis step then reports that no published evidence exists for those two subtopics.
The team wants the smallest change that stops these false negatives, while keeping the three good results.
What is it?
Take a second.
The answer.
Subagents return failures distinctly from empty results, with error_class, retryability, and coverage counts.
That lets the coordinator do three things.
Keep the good results.
Retry the transient failures, within a bound.
And propagate any remaining gap.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: have the synthesis agent lower its confidence, and add a caveat when a subtopic looks thin.
Why?
It doesn't name the gap.
So the subtopics still read as searched and empty.
Wrong: discard everything and restart all five whenever any comes back short.
Why?
It throws away three good results.
That's the exact waste a partial-result contract exists to prevent.
Wrong: raise the timeout, and retry every failed search until it returns at least one result.
Why?
That's an unbounded retry.
And it also pressures the system to manufacture findings, where a true empty was possible.
Hold on to this line.
An empty result is not a success.
"Not searched" and "nothing found" must look different when they cross the boundary.
Takeaway.
Failures cross agent boundaries as structured facts.
Never as prose.
And never disguised as empty results.
The second concept is vocabulary.
The plain version.
Imagine every hospital department used its own word for urgent.
The triage desk would spend its day translating, and still get some wrong.
One shared set of labels changes that.
Say urgent, routine, and needs authorisation.
The desk can route instantly.
And a notes field keeps the detail for the doctor.
In exam terms, use the same error class vocabulary at the agent layer that the tool layer already uses.
The earlier chapter on tool design classifies tool failures three ways.
Transient.
Business.
And permission.
Reuse exactly those three values in the subagent's failure objects.
The error_class field tells the coordinator what to do.
Transient gets a bounded retry.
Business changes the plan.
Permission escalates.
The situational detail goes in a separate error_code field.
Things like auth_denied, or upstream_timeout, or tenant_boundary.
And that one is for the human.
So a permission failure routes to escalation whether its code says auth_denied or tenant_boundary.
That is the whole point of a taxonomy.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A CI coordinator delegates dependency, licence and secrets scans to three subagents.
Each invented its own failure labels: ACCESS_PROBLEM, flaky, blocked, denied_maybe.
And the coordinator keeps retrying authorisation failures, while escalating simple timeouts.
The tools already classify their own errors.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Report error_class with the tool layer's three values, and put the detail in error_code.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep the invented labels, and add a translation table in the coordinator.
Why?
That's exactly the cost a shared vocabulary avoids.
And it breaks every time a new label appears.
Wrong: return plain-language descriptions, and let the coordinator's model decide from the wording.
Why?
That's the rumour problem again.
Wrong: collapse everything into one retryable true-or-false flag.
Why?
It loses the difference between business and permission failures.
Both are non-retryable.
But they need different actions.
Takeaway.
One error vocabulary across every layer. error_class decides the action. error_code records what happened.
The third concept is retry discipline.
It ties the first two together.
The plain version.
If a door is locked, knocking harder does not help.
Knocking again helps only if someone might have been in the shower.
So before you try again, you need to know which kind of problem it was.
In exam terms.
Hold on to this line.
Classification overrides the retry counter.
A failure classified as non-retryable is never retried.
No matter how much budget remains.
An authorisation failure, an HTTP four-oh-three, reproduces identically forever.
The notes use three attempts per unit as their house number.
And they're explicit that this is house guidance, not a platform limit.
The retry_would_help_if field turns "should I retry?" from a guess into a lookup.
For example: retry would help if the token is granted read access on that repository.
Question three.
This one is select two.
Here's the scenario, from the notes.
A subagent could not read a private repository's manifest.
The coordinator retried three times, got the same failure, and reported no vulnerabilities across four repositories.
Which two changes are correct?
Take a second.
The answers.
And notice they fix two separate defects.
First.
A structured failure, with class, retryability, and the unblocking condition.
So the permission failure is not retried.
Second.
Coverage counts, plus the names of the unexamined repositories, in the human-facing report.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the retry limit to six, with exponential backoff.
Why?
It treats a deterministic failure as transient.
And it makes the waste worse.
Wrong: lower the report's confidence from high to medium.
Why?
The security team still treats the unread repository as clean.
Takeaway.
Never retry what is classified non-retryable.
Name the condition that would unblock it instead.
Which brings us to the coordinator's side of the bargain.
And the word the notes use for getting it wrong: laundering.
The plain version.
A team assistant receives a note saying "thirty-six of forty files checked, four were illegible."
Then the assistant tells the boss, "none of the forty files had the problem."
Every word the assistant received was accurate.
The gap vanished at the last step.
In exam terms, the coordinator must propagate the coverage gap into its own output.
Not absorb it.
Hold on to this line.
Error propagation that stops one level short of the human is not propagation.
It is laundering.
So the report has to do three things.
Say eleven of thirteen, or thirty-six of forty.
Name the missing units.
And say why.
Why the why?
Because the unblocking action is often the most useful output of the whole run.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A contract-extraction coordinator sends forty contracts out.
One subagent returns a well-formed partial result.
Thirty-six extracted.
Four failed on unreadable scans.
And a claim_scope saying those four were not examined.
The coordinator then tells the legal team, "no change-of-control clauses found across the forty contracts."
Where is the defect?
Take a second.
The answer.
In the coordinator.
The subagent did its job perfectly.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: blame the subagent for not retrying the unreadable scans.
Why?
An unreadable scan fails the same way every time.
And the subagent already reported correctly.
Wrong: add "medium confidence" to the report.
Why?
It doesn't say which four contracts were skipped.
Wrong: have the coordinator re-extract all forty itself.
Why?
That's the named anti-pattern of a coordinator re-reading what its subagents read.
It pays full cost twice, and still doesn't fix how the gap is reported.
And the notes stress why this is a reliability defect, rather than a wording nicety.
Legal and security teams act on absence of findings.
So, a contrast.
Is it a subagent defect, or a coordinator defect?
Ask where the information about the gap last existed.
If the subagent returned prose, or a fake empty success, the defect is in the subagent's contract.
If the subagent returned a correct partial result, and the gap disappeared in the summary, the defect is in the coordinator.
That's part three.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Lowering confidence is not naming the gap.
The human-facing report says how many of how many, and which ones.
Coming up in part four: managing context in large codebase exploration.
